title: Naso: confess and repay (Numbers 5:6–7)
hook: a wrong is confessed aloud and repaid with a fifth added

segments.voice: Yesterday: naso, lift up the head, and your line, counting is lifting. Did someone who carries the soft loads get a specific thank-you? Day four hundred thirty-seven.

You borrowed your neighbor's ladder in March and it's now October. Or you dinged a friend's car door in a parking lot and drove off, and it's been nagging for a year. You could just quietly return the ladder. You could slip some cash in an envelope. It's tempting to fix things in a way that skips saying anything out loud. Today's verses in Naso describe how a wrong gets fixed, and they include two steps that are easy to skip. One of them is your mouth. The other is your wallet, plus a little.
screen: `A LADDER KEPT SINCE MARCH.` → `FIX IT QUIETLY?` → `YOUR MOUTH, AND A LITTLE EXTRA.`

segments.voice: Numbers five, verses six and seven. When a man or a woman wrongs another person, the Torah calls it a trespass against the LORD. Notice that: cheating your neighbor isn't only between the two of you. Then comes the remedy: "then they shall confess their sin which they have done." After that, they repay the full amount, add a fifth on top, and give it to the person they wronged. Two steps, in order. First, the mouth. Then the money. The verse's verb is vehitvadu, they shall confess, and from it comes the name for this first step: vidui, confession, owning it. Maimonides builds a whole teaching on this verse. Real repentance, he writes, includes saying it in words: I did this, I regret it, I'm ashamed of it, I won't do it again. Thinking it isn't enough. The words make it real, to you as much as anyone. On Yom Kippur, the confessions are said aloud, together, in the plural: we have sinned, we have done wrong. Then the fifth. Returning what you took only puts things back where they were. The added fifth admits that the other person lost more than an object. They lost time, trust, sleep, the use of their ladder all summer. The rabbis worked out the arithmetic: the fifth is counted so that it's a fifth of the total you hand over. And if the wronged person has died with no relatives, the verse says, the payment doesn't vanish. It goes to the priest. A debt like this doesn't just expire.
screen: `A WRONG TO A NEIGHBOR, A TRESPASS.` · `FIRST THE MOUTH: VIDUI.` · `SAY IT IN WORDS.` · `THEN THE MONEY, PLUS A FIFTH.` · then, large: `REPAY, AND ADD A FIFTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one amends with a bit extra. Breathe, and look for one small wrong you still owe for: the ladder, a forgotten favor, a loan, a cutting remark. Picture the person. First, find the words you'd say, short and plain: I did this, and I'm sorry. Say them silently. Then think of the fifth: the extra that admits their loss. A coffee with the returned book. A full tank with the borrowed car. The bell holds the time.
Vidui. Confession: owning a wrong out loud, the first step before repaying it, and the root of the Yom Kippur prayers.
Your line: repay, and add a fifth. Today, make the amends you pictured, words first, then the return, with a little extra. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition sees verbal confession, vidui, as part of repentance; on Yom Kippur the congregation recites the confessions together, aloud and in the plural, and wrongs against people are repaired by making restitution and seeking their forgiveness.

notes: 'then they shall confess their sin which they have done' from JPS 1917 Numbers 5:7, from memory; confirm.
The added fifth: the rabbinic reckoning is 'a fifth from outside', so the fifth is a fifth of the total (a quarter of the principal). Confirm source (Bava Metzia 54a) and the simplified phrasing.
Maimonides' elements of confession paraphrased (Laws of Repentance 1:1; 2:2).
Vidui root y-d-h (to acknowledge, confess) is standard; the script says 'to acknowledge, to own'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what 'most of us would love'; vidui is now tied to the verse's own verb (vehitvadu) instead of an etymology claim; the causal 'that's why on Yom Kippur' softened to a plain description; a myth reveal's 'never' softened.
